title: Sandra Lovelace v. Northeast Presbytery
disposition_detail: The SJC approved the panel's unanimous decision that Lovelace's October 11, 1990 and January 23, 1991 letters did not constitute complaints administratively or judicially in order, for distinct BCO 43 filing and complainable-action defects.
first_summary: The SJC found two attempted complaints administratively and judicially out of order. The October 1990 filing did not satisfy BCO 43-2 because the earlier letters it invoked had merely asked questions or communicated concern, rather than first presenting a complaint to Presbytery, and concerned an oral report not made part of Presbytery's record. The January 1991 filing supplied no supporting reasons as BCO 43-3 required and challenged specifications of error that were not themselves acts or decisions of Presbytery.

sources.supports: Case identity, two letters at issue, dual out-of-order dispositions, distinct reasons under BCO 43-2 and 43-3, panel unanimity, and SJC approval.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: Lines 14-18 identify Judicial Case 91-1 and the complaint; lines 46-54 identify the unanimous judicial panel decision and its approval by the SJC.
evidence_notes.dispute: Lines 20-30 ask whether Lovelace's October 11, 1990 and January 23, 1991 letters constituted complaints administratively and judicially in order against alleged Presbytery actions.
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: Lines 32-42 find both letters administratively and judicially out of order. The October filing failed the first-presentation requirement because the June letters were not complaints and the oral report was not in Presbytery's record; the January filing lacked supporting reasons and did not identify complainable acts or decisions.
evidence_notes.qualifications: The ruling addresses the procedural validity of the two letters, not the merits of the concerns or of the four specifications Presbytery had declined to sustain.
